cases.claim: Wiring `daemon-soak` to something real is then a small piece of work with a defect already waiting for it, rather than a bookkeeping question.
cases.evidence: Three of them are one cluster and the fourth is a different question. `daemon-soak.sh` (550 lines), `daemon-soak-report.sh` (117) and `daemon-supervised.sh` (41) all last moved on 2026-08-10 and all point at `sovereign/docs/specs/DAEMON_RESILIENCE.md`. The soak boots a real daemon in an isolated HOME on non-default ports with small models and drives the failure modes the P0 hardening was supposed to make boring. The report reads a live install's supervisor log, crash records and rotated `daemon.err` and renders a ship/no-ship verdict. `daemon-supervised.sh` is the odd one — it isn't a check at all, it's the in-toolbox supervisor that relaunches the daemon on the RSS exit-102 and lost-listener exit-104 paths. It's the thing that runs the daemon, not a thing that verifies it, so `by-hand` is arguably the wrong shape for it in a different way than the others. `mesh-soak.sh` (1,251 lines, last moved 2026-08-26) is separate. Its own header describes a three-layer mesh QA stack: Layer 1 is the in-process DST, Layer 3 is `sovereign mesh soak-gate`, and this is Layer 2, the "real bytes" layer that boots N real daemons over TCP gossip and SIGKILLs them in cycles. Layer 1 is now wired to `ci:test` as `dst-scenarios`. Layer 3 isn't in the registry at all. So the middle layer being unwired isn't a lone straggler — it's the visible half of a QA stack that's two-thirds unwired. The reason this matters beyond bookkeeping: entry 3 on the product-defect stack is the daemon being jetsam-killed by *two* concurrent chat turns, twice in ten minutes, with clients seeing a bare `Inference error`. That is precisely what `daemon-soak.sh` exists to catch, and it caught nothing because nothing ran it. The registry's own founding postmortem — `wizard-verify.sh` referenced by prose and by nothing executable, having caught a ship-blocking bug on its first run — is the same story. My recommendation shifts on that. Rather than sorting which of the four a human theoretically runs, treat the honest answer as `[]` for all four and let the gap number say what it means: this repo has a daemon-resilience suite and a mesh soak layer that nothing schedules, and it just paid for it.

cases.claim: The headline: `sovereign-cli-daemon` has zero direct `commonwealth-*` deps.
cases.evidence: Phase 3 is complete — 3a, 3b, 3c all landed. The bar's own instrument reached target on class 1, and the bar moved 3.0 → 2.0. But the more useful result is what reaching target exposed. The bar's prose claim is not met, and it's further away than the number suggests. The daemon still pulls ten commonwealth crates *transitively*, all through `sovereign-mesh`, because it reaches 78 distinct `sovereign_mesh::` items. The instrument asks "direct"; the claim says "zero". Only the first got answered, and that gap was invisible while the number was still moving. That's K2's fusion at a new address. K2 feared local and mesh state were welded at `AppState` — they aren't; the daemon has zero type refs to it, and `ConvergenceRecord` turned out to be two `Option<i64>` behind a mutex. The real weld is `daemon → sovereign-mesh`, 78 items wide. By K2's own logic that's either the next seam or a runtime profile, and it's a phase, not a rung. 3b refused the iroh half with data, and was right to. Not "one line each": 17 errors from the manifest change alone, 28 more after cfg-gating, and decisively — the no-iroh arm would have no consumer while the daemon can't drop `sovereign-mesh`, so nothing would ever build it. A cfg-split join path that never runs in production is K11's failure moved from runtime to compile time. iroh leaves with the mesh. Three errors in the order I wrote, all found by measurement: My gate command could never pass. `cargo tree … | grep -c '^commonwealth-'` has no `--depth`, so it counts the whole tree — it asked a different question than the bar does. Class 2 is one forcing, not two. `sovereign-server` isn't in the daemon's tree at all; the floor_basis counted it anyway. The mesh-mint doesn't "die for free," and my reasoning was wrong. `create_mesh` persists node identity, builds the mesh record, *starts the listener*, and stamps the invite; its `return 1` fires on real failures a solo node hits. A solo *adapter* constructs infallibly — a solo *node* still needs a listener. Two things 3b caught that were better than my instructions. My order said the solo convergence impl should report "always converged"; it instead reports `None` for a path that has never run — because "converged" for something that never ran is a defaulted absence (§18.3). And its red-watch found that `should_host_is_true_for_a_roster_of_one` was the only one of partition's fifteen tests that went red under sabotage: the degenerate roster the entire local-daemon design rests on was untested. Also fell out for free: `sovereign-work-atlas` left the substrate too — a capabilities crate that needed two commonwealth crates for four store methods that all have a correct N=1 answer. I'll report the sweep verdict when it lands.

The substrate (`core`, `transport`, `state`, `discovery`, `rail`, `rail-core`), the mesh API (`commonwealth-api`), and two crates that carry the prefix and nothing else. You cannot read the domain boundary off a manifest. That's the root problem, and it's exactly why the daemon bar can't be measured honestly. Note `91898eef` records `commonwealth-tdd` as a false positive on that rule's first real run — the classifier saw a `commonwealth-` crate reaching into sovereign and called it backflow. The rule got weakened to fit the name. A standing exemption in the layer map, `ARCH_LAYERS.toml:261`: *"commonwealth-agent-tools + commonwealth-tdd live in sovereign/crates/ (naming predates the monorepo merge) — their sovereign deps are exempted here… since the crates are sovereign-side in all but name."* That exemption exists solely because the names lie. The daemon bar's instrument counts by prefix, so it reports ≥1 forever, even at true zero. And the same note that recorded cost 1 states the principle that condemns cost 2: *"an exception written against a true positive is how a gate becomes decorative, and one written against a false positive is a lie in the map."* The `:261` exemption is that lie, written by the person who named the rule. The moves are small and the placement is nearly right already: `commonwealth-agent-tools` → `sovereign-agent-tools`. It's already in the `capabilities` layer (line 225), the lone `commonwealth-` name among ten `sovereign-*` crates. Layer correct, name wrong. `commonwealth-tdd` → `sovereign-tdd`, and move it out of the `mesh-api` layer into `capabilities`. Its dependents are `sovereign-server`, `sovereign-cli-daemon`, `sovereign-agent-bench` — all sovereign, all hosts. Delete the `:261` exemption. That last one is the falsifier, and I'd make it the rung's success criterion: the rename succeeds if the exemption can be deleted, not if the crates get new names. If something still needs exempting afterwards, the boundary was somewhere else and we found that out cheaply. One constraint to carry: `commonwealth-tdd` backs two shipped MCP tools, `tdd_solve` and `tdd_bdd_cycle`, served into `tools/list`. Those ids are a wire surface. The crate renames; the tool ids must not. How this answers the layering question. After the rename, `commonwealth-` means exactly one thing, and `grep '^commonwealth-' Cargo.toml` becomes a true test of substrate coupling — which is precisely what the local-only-daemon bar's instrument is trying to be and currently can't. Combined with the two ports, the boundary stops needing a build to prove and becomes something `boundary-gate` can see mechanically: *a local-only daemon is a package whose closure contains zero `commonwealth-*`.* So the phase has a natural order, cheapest and most clarifying first: rename and re-place the two crates (deletes an exemption, makes the instrument honest, and drops the daemon's count from 4 to 3 without touching a line of daemon logic) → dissolve the two neutral couplings (`kernel_types::NodeId` directly; the pure partition functions down a layer) → the two ports with the honest N=1 solo adapter → iroh propagation. Only the third step is design work; the rest is putting things where they belong. Want me to write this up as the Phase 3 order?

cases.claim: The plan was to make the coverage probe read `raptor_summaries.lance` and the atlas seed table instead of only `chunks.lance`.
cases.evidence: Interim, while the full test run finishes — the analysis is done and it changes the plan. The frame's top-ranked fix is wrong, and I can show it. I measured all three layers against all 43 `secret_agent` questions: `max(chunk, raptor, atoms)` crosses the 0.55 floor for zero questions that `chunk` alone did not. The probe is also correct in both directions on the live run — embassy 0.6605 → ClaimUncovered, Berlin Wall 0.3003 → TopicUncovered. It is a fix with no failing input; I did not build it. The real defect is one layer down, and it is much larger than one probe. `section_extraction_kinds()` emits Entity, State, Relation, Event, Claim, Question. No built-in navigation row named Event, Relation or Question — and `seed_population` derives the ANN seed table from the union of the rows' seed kinds. So those three kinds never got a vector, could never be seeded, and were unreachable even by the unfiltered row, which seeds from that same table. On `chaos-secret-agent`, `atlas status --json` reported `ann.embedded_atoms` 151 against 226 atoms; the missing 75 are exactly Event 33 + Relation 20 + Question 22. Fleet-wide it is worse: `dopesick_jesus` 543 of 1,181, `enron-sample-multi-wide` 2,789 of 6,101. That is why the killer-weapon probe fails. The answer is `event-0033` — "Mrs Verloc stabs Mr Verloc in the breast with a carving knife", evidence `sec_0011`. It scores 0.5627 on that question; the `Mr Verloc` entity the seeder did admit scores 0.3659. The corpus held the answer, the model produced it from memory, and the value-presence veto correctly refused it because the evidence never contained it. The existing ratchet proved rows ⊆ emits. Nothing proved the converse, so a third of every build could vanish in silence. Landed: `render_atom_entry` gains Event and Relation arms, the `lookup` row seeds them in all four section-extraction genres and the pre-registered table, `SEED_POPULATION_SCHEMA` 2→3, and a new ratchet `every_kind_a_pipeline_emits_is_reachable_by_some_row` — watched to fail on "drop Event from literary lookup". On its first run it found a second orphan: engineering emitted Configuration with every row that could reach one switched off, so `runs_configuration_phase()` is now false there. Measured effect after `atlas migrate-all chaos-secret-agent`: embedded atoms 151 → 204, `event-0033` seeded at rank 6, and the retrieval window changed — the leaf set stopped being entirely early-novel. The probe still abstains. It stops at a precisely located next defect: literary evidence links are section ids (`sec_0011`), so `ChunkSelector::parse` yields Section and the by-row fetch is unavailable; the walk resolves each request by searching the atom's `passage_preview` text, and those results lose the merge to base retrieval. That is note `8e608436`'s named defect with the fetch side now working, and unlike the two existing reserve lanes these chunks are cosine-scored, so pinning them overrides a ranking rather than repairing a demotion — a design call with a both-directions measurement owed, not a one-liner. Also landed: `coverage_near_sim` 0.55 → 0.49, labelled as the threshold move it is. 0.55 sat inside the in-topic band, which is what let `distract-bomb-maker` (0.5475, squarely in-corpus) read TopicUncovered and let `gk_rescue` put a wrong parametric answer in front of the reader. The boundary is now the top of the observed off-topic band across both calibration runs; the classes separate in a 0.019-wide gap, and the doc comment says so. Full lint passed (exit 0, workspace). Test run in flight; I will commit once it returns and report the counts.

cases.claim: I changed it because 0.55 sat inside the measured in-topic band and that is what let `distract-bomb-maker` read TopicUncovered and leak a wrong parametric answer.
cases.evidence: The lane is still red, and I want to be exact about which parts moved. What is comprehensively fixed is one *class* of defect, not the failing probe. "A pipeline emits an atom kind that no navigation row can reach" is now structurally impossible to reintroduce quietly: the converse ratchet covers all five built-in genres, I watched it fail on a named input, and it caught a second instance I wasn't looking for (engineering's Phase 8). Until that is fixed, `present-killer-weapon` stays a false abstention and RED-LINE 1 stays at 0.00. The coverage-floor change is in a weaker state than that: correct at the definition, unverified end to end. I have not re-run the smoke subset to watch the leak stop. And even when it does stop, it converts a wrong answer into an abstention — it does not make the answer correct, so it does not move competence either. The one thing it should move is "wrong answers reaching the reader: 1 → 0", which is the cardinal-sin axis. Three things I found and did not fix. And the merge defect above is a design call — unlike the two existing reserve lanes, these chunks are cosine-scored, so pinning them overrides a ranking rather than repairing a demotion, and that needs a both-directions measurement I did not have time to run. So: one class closed, one threshold corrected but unwitnessed, one root cause located to a specific line of the fetch path, and the lane unchanged. The honest scoreboard is that tonight bought a correct diagnosis and a structural guard, not a green gate. The measurement I owe is the 4-probe smoke subset re-run with both changes in.
